Our static-site release has two steps. First, we upload all new assets under versioned names. Then we switch the manifest to point at those names. We never delete or overwrite the old assets as part of a release.

**Why the upload comes first:** The manifest is what browsers follow, so every name in it must already exist when it goes live. If we switched first, browsers could load the new manifest and request assets that haven't been uploaded yet, getting 404s and a broken page.

**Why we keep the old assets:** A browser that fetched the previous manifest before the switch will keep requesting the old asset names. Leaving those files in place lets that browser finish loading a consistent old version instead of breaking partway through.

Every release happens in two steps: we upload the new assets, then we switch the manifest to point at them.

First, we upload every new asset under a versioned name, such as `app.3f9c2a.js`, so it never overwrites an existing file. Once all of them are uploaded, we update the manifest to reference the new names. The manifest switch is the moment the release goes live.

The upload has to finish first because the manifest makes a promise that those files exist. If we switched the manifest first, a browser could fetch it and then request a script or stylesheet that hasn't arrived yet. That request would return a 404 and the page would break. Uploading first means every name in the new manifest already resolves by the time anyone can see it.

We keep the old assets because browsers don't all move to the new release at the same moment. A visitor who loaded the page before the switch is still running the previous manifest. Any asset that page loads later, such as a lazy-loaded chunk or a font, will be requested under the old versioned name. Deleting the old files would break those sessions partway through. Because the names are versioned, the old and new files can sit side by side without conflict. Both releases keep working until the old sessions end.

Our releases happen in two steps. First we upload every new asset under a versioned name. Then we switch the manifest to point at those names.

A release has two steps: upload every new asset under a versioned name, then switch the manifest to point at those names. Because each version gets a new name, a release never overwrites a file that a browser might already be using.

The upload comes first so the manifest never references a file that doesn't exist yet. Once the manifest switches, any browser that loads it will immediately request the new asset names. If those files were still uploading, the browser would get 404s and render a broken page. Finishing the upload first means the switch is the only moment the live site changes, and every name it points to is already in place.

We keep the old assets because switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that have already loaded the previous one. Those browsers keep requesting the old names for lazy-loaded scripts, code-split chunks, images and fonts until the user reloads. If we deleted the old files at release time, those users would hit 404s mid-session. Keeping the old files lets every open session finish on the version it started with.
